gap.headline: Your four units add up to genuinely strong fundamentals; what stands between you and a Software Developer offer is production practice — Git, the web stack, one deployed project.

capabilities.name: Programming fundamentals

evidence.quote: design and write basic programs using a high-level procedural programming language

capabilities.rationale: Your first programming unit covers exactly what employers mean by fundamentals, and you can point to it.

capabilities.name: C and systems-level programming

evidence.quote: introduces students to a system programming language that gives programmers this kind of control

evidence.unitTitle: Intro. to Numerical Computation in C
evidence.quote: key elements of programming in a high level language

capabilities.rationale: You have written real C, which is more low-level exposure than most graduates bring.

capabilities.name: Data structures and algorithms

evidence.quote: explores a range of standard data structures and algorithmic techniques
introduced to the most frequently used data structures and their associated algorithms

capabilities.rationale: Two units of data structures and algorithms is genuine depth — interviewers call this 'strong DSA fundamentals'.

capabilities.name: Reasoning about performance and correctness

evidence.quote: justification of algorithm correctness, on analysis of algorithm performance

capabilities.rationale: You have been examined on arguing correctness and analysing performance, which is what technical interviews test.

capabilities.name: Testing discipline

evidence.unitTitle: Intro. to Numerical Computation in C
evidence.quote: implement appropriate testing regimes to allow validation and debugging of those programs

capabilities.rationale: You have planned testing regimes for numerical code, but not with a framework or in a team codebase.

capabilities.name: Debugging real programs

evidence.quote: Read, write, test and debug typical small-scale programs

capabilities.rationale: You debug your own small programs; production debugging in an unfamiliar codebase is a step further.

capabilities.name: Git and version control
capabilities.rationale: No unit teaches it, every team expects it, and it is the single cheapest gap on this list to close.

capabilities.name: JavaScript, HTML and CSS
capabilities.rationale: Software developer ads in Australia ask for the web stack more than any other technology, and your degree has not touched it yet.

capabilities.name: SQL and relational databases
capabilities.rationale: Almost every backend role assumes you can model and query data; nothing on your transcript covers it yet.

capabilities.name: A cloud platform (AWS or Azure)
capabilities.rationale: In-demand in the ads and absent from coursework — one deployed project is how students usually close this.

capabilities.name: Docker, containers and CI
capabilities.rationale: This is production practice, not course content; a small pipeline on your own project is enough to talk about it.

capabilities.name: Linux and the command line

evidence.unitTitle: Intro. to Numerical Computation in C
evidence.quote: Design, develop, and implement typical small-scale numerical programs

capabilities.rationale: Working in C puts you near the command line, but day-to-day Linux fluency is still assumed, not taught.

capabilities.name: Working in a team codebase
capabilities.rationale: Group work is not the same as branching, code review and merging — the workflow every employer runs.

capabilities.name: Explaining technical decisions

evidence.unitTitle: Intro. to Numerical Computation in C
evidence.quote: Develop and present arguments relating to the correctness of such programs

capabilities.rationale: Coursework makes you justify decisions in writing; doing it for a non-technical audience is the remaining step.

roadmap.headline: One semester left means triage: only what makes you credible for the roles you are applying to right now.
roadmap.stageNote: This plan is built for a final-year with one semester: it drops foundations there is no longer time for and spends everything on evidence employers can open. A first-year with the same gaps would get a six-semester arc instead.

steps.title: Move your COMP20003 and COMP20005 work into Git this week and make the repos public
steps.rationale: A day of work that converts four units of coursework into evidence a recruiter can actually open.

steps.title: Build one small web app on top of your algorithms work — a route-finder or data explorer — and deploy it to a free cloud tier
steps.rationale: One deployed project is the single strongest signal you can add in a semester, and it reuses the unit you are best at.

steps.title: Write tests for that project with a real framework and wire up CI on the repo
steps.rationale: You already know testing regimes from numerical computing — naming the framework is what job ads screen for.

steps.title: Attend MelbJS and one Junior Dev meetup before applications close, and talk about the project you just shipped
steps.rationale: Referrals beat cold applications, these rooms contain the people who give them, and you now have something concrete to say.

steps.title: Deliberately left out: Docker depth, Linux fluency, a second language — name them in interviews as next
steps.rationale: Saying plainly what you cut and why reads as judgement, not weakness — the thing one semester cannot buy is breadth.
